caption:
The diagram depicts a two-dimensional representation of the Penrose triangle, also known as the "impossible triangle" or "impossible tribar." It is an optical illusion consisting of an object which can be depicted in a perspective drawing, but cannot exist as a solid object. It consists of three straight beams of square cross-section which meet pairwise at right angles at the vertices of the triangle they form.

The Penrose triangle is arranged in such a way that if one were to follow the surface of one of the beams, it would loop back on itself in a continuous path, creating the illusion of a three-dimensional object. The beams are shaded and drawn with perspective to enhance the illusion of three-dimensionality, with one side of each beam appearing darker to imply shadow and depth.

In a mathematical or problem-solving context, the Penrose triangle is often used to illustrate concepts of perspective, three-dimensional representation on two-dimensional surfaces, and the limitations of human visual perception. However, since it is an impossible object, it cannot be used as a basis for realistic physical construction or mathematical calculation pertaining to real-world geometry.
